text: Every AWS account has a Billing and Cost Management console — the actual bill, invoices, payment methods, and a running total for the current period. It's the source of truth for what's being charged. But reading a total doesn't explain it, which is where Cost Explorer comes in: a tool for visualizing that spend over time instead of just staring at one number and guessing why it moved.

The Cost Explorer API, get-cost-and-usage, is the same data the console chart is built from. Given a start and end date, a monthly granularity, and grouped by service, it returns exactly what's driving the bill, service by service — the same breakdown Cost Explorer renders as a chart, except available from the CLI or a script, which matters once this becomes a recurring check rather than a one-off look.

Cost Explorer lets you group or filter spend by service — EC2, S3, RDS, and the rest — to see what's actually costing money. By linked account, once an AWS Organization has more than one account under it. By Region, to see where the spend is physically happening. And by tag, which is where Chapter 5's tagging discipline pays off directly: attributing cost to a specific project or team that spans several services at once, something a service-only view could never answer cleanly on its own.

Cost Explorer's forecast extrapolates from past usage patterns, shown by default alongside the last several months of actual spend — it's genuinely good at catching a spending trend early, flagging that this month is on pace to blow past last month's number well before the bill closes. What it can't do is see a brand-new project or migration nobody's told it about yet. It's trend extrapolation, not prophecy, and it's worth remembering which one you're looking at.

A spike from roughly $600 to $1,100 gets traced in two clicks: group the current month by service first, find EC2 is nearly all of the increase, then filter to EC2 only and group by tag to find the specific project responsible for that usage. Next, Lesson 26 covers setting a budget so that kind of spike gets flagged automatically by AWS itself, before anyone has to go looking for the cause by hand.
